correspondences.rationale: Both denote an OTN switching resource with an ODU cross-connect fabric.
Both denote the customer-facing port that maps or terminates a client signal in an ODU.
The VC launch OFA is the amplifier at the transmitting end of an optical multiplex or wavelength section.
Both denote an intermediate inline optical amplifier between terminal sites.
The VC landing OFA is the receiving-end preamplifier of the optical section.
Both are optical routing resources that use wavelength-selective switching to steer individual channels.
Both map one client service onto one line wavelength.
Both aggregate multiple lower-rate client services onto one line wavelength.
Both denote an OTN line interface connected to an ODU switching fabric.
Both are hard failures of an OTN cross-connect switching fabric.
Both describe an incorrectly configured OTN cross-connect delivering an ODU to the wrong destination.
Both are failures of a client-facing port or its optic.
Both describe a hard amplifier or pump failure resulting in no optical output.
Both mean amplifier gain has fallen below its configured value.
Both describe increased amplifier-added noise or noise figure with degraded OSNR.
Both denote pump ageing evidenced by gradually increasing pump drive current.
Both mean amplifier gain is no longer flat across the optical band.
Both denote a complete physical fibre break that prevents light from passing.
Both denote an increase in fibre-span loss caused by effects such as bends or stressed cable.
Both denote a disconnected connector or optical patch cord.
Both concern excessive channel-specific attenuation at a wavelength-selective switch, although A emphasizes exceeding compensation range.
Both denote a wavelength-selective switch passband shifted away from the channel frequency.
Both describe failure of a wavelength-router or WSS directional port affecting all light entering there.
Both denote failure of a coherent transmitter laser, leaving its optical output dark.
Both denote hard failure of the complete terminal card or module.
Both are receiver-local degradations that add a decoding penalty without implicating the route.
Both denote transmitter laser ageing observed as upward drift in bias current.
Both describe a slow decline in an optical channel's performance margin.
Both denote increasing differential group delay on the optical path.
Both denote a rapid transient change in optical state of polarization.
Both denote connector contamination that introduces optical loss or penalty.
Both denote absence of detectable optical signal or power below detection threshold.
Both mean received optical signal power is reduced or below the required level.
Both denote loss of the span optical supervisory channel, which is terminated and regenerated at amplifier sites.
Both mean the optical signal has reduced OSNR because of added noise.
Both describe a fast state-of-polarization change; A additionally states that it exceeds receiver tracking speed.
Both mean differential group delay is elevated beyond acceptable tolerance.
Both denote filter narrowing or misalignment that reduces signal quality while power may remain normal.
Both denote a receiver-local penalty that does not propagate through the network.
Both denote loss of OTU frame alignment at the line receiver.
Both denote pre-FEC errors above the degradation threshold while frame alignment remains available.
Both concern ODU Alarm Indication Signal propagating downstream on an ODU path; A expresses the receiving condition.
Both mean an ODU has been delivered to a destination other than its intended endpoint.
Both denote interruption of the client or customer service.
Both denote the brief client interruption caused by a protection switch.
Both describe pump drive current rising as the amplifier pump ages.
Both describe transmit-laser bias current rising with age.
Both denote a channel margin that declines slowly.
Both are total optical power measured at an amplifier input.
Both are total optical power measured at an amplifier output.
Both measure amplifier pump drive current as a percentage of its commissioning or beginning-of-life reference.
Both measure transmitter laser bias as a percentage of its commissioning or beginning-of-life reference.
Both are per-channel optical-power measurements at a wavelength router or ROADM channel monitor.
Both are per-channel OSNR measurements at a wavelength router or ROADM channel monitor.
Both denote optical power measured at a line receiver.
Both denote line errored-second performance counts; B explicitly specifies 15-minute reporting bins.
Both are receiver-DSP estimates of optical signal-to-noise ratio.
Both are the coherent receiver's pre-FEC bit error ratio.
Both are receiver estimates of differential group delay.
Both measure the rate of change of received state of polarization.
Both count client errored seconds; B explicitly packages the count in 15-minute bins.
Both count client unavailable seconds; B explicitly packages the count in 15-minute bins.
Both scopes cover every optical channel in the affected multiplexed signal.
Both scopes identify one optical channel.
Both scope an impairment to a subset of channels rather than the complete multiplex, with A specifically identifying a band edge.
Both scopes cover every wavelength arriving through one ROADM or wavelength-router directional input port.
Both scope a statement to the equipment unit or module itself rather than only its traffic.
Both restrict an impairment to the current receiver only.
Both scopes cover every ODU cross-connected through the switch.
Both scopes identify one ODU.
Both scopes identify the particular client or customer service.
Both locate the condition at the specific unit or module that reported it.
Both locate the condition at the particular client or tributary port raising the alarm.
Both denote the fibre span immediately upstream of and feeding the current unit.
Both denote the amplifier immediately before the span feeding the current unit.
Both identify the input patch or connection at the transmitting head of the optical multiplex section.
Both cover any upstream fibre, amplifier, section input, or router point earlier on the same optical path.
Both cover the end-to-end signal path including the remote line interface, though their descriptions use opposite observation orientations.
Both denote either client-side endpoint of the carried service.
Both denote an OTN switch or cross-connect located on the service's ODU path.
Both denote the preferred or working ODU path used under normal operation.
Both denote the alternate protection ODU path.
Both denote the ODU path currently carrying the service, whether working or protection.
Both denote the standard monitoring entitlement present without optional telemetry packs.
Both denote the optional capability exposing optical input, output, and receive-power measurements.
Both provide per-channel power and OSNR measurements at optical routing equipment.
Both provide advanced coherent-DSP and equipment-health telemetry such as OSNR, DGD, pump current, and laser bias.
Both classify an abrupt fault that makes traffic or the affected resource unavailable.
Both classify a fault where traffic remains present but signal quality is reduced.
Both are the highest operational severity for conditions requiring immediate response.
Both denote a significant alarm below the highest urgency level.
Both denote a lower-priority warning or maintenance condition.
Both describe a reported informational condition that is not treated as an actionable alarm.
Both mean an arriving condition or carried content is forwarded unchanged.
Both describe independent per-channel routing, with line-wide conditions continuing on each routed channel.
